lines.text: Do you know how a barcode works? Those black stripes are just a number, written in light and dark.
The scanner shines red light across it. White gaps bounce it back, black bars swallow it, so the sensor sees a rhythm of flashes.
Each digit takes seven thin slots, made of two bars and two gaps. Their widths spell out zero to nine.
The stripes hold no price and no name. Just a number. The shop's computer looks it up, and finds what you're buying.
The last digit is a check. It's worked out from all the others, so if one stripe is misread, the sum fails, and the scanner won't beep.
It even reads upside down. The left and right halves use different patterns, so the scanner knows which end is which.
The first thing ever scanned at a checkout was a pack of chewing gum, in Ohio, in 1974.
Orbi puts the barcode's square cousin on every file you send. Your friend scans the QR code and lands right on the file. Add a code, and only people who know it can open it.
